summary: Kwindla Hultman Kramer, CEO of Daily (real-time audio/video infrastructure), presents on building fast voice AI bots at the AI Engineer World's Fair. The talk addresses two core challenges: architectural flexibility and latency. The stack spans audio processing (echo cancellation, CPU management), networking, transcription, phrase endpointing, interruption handling with state management, LLM inference, TTS, and tool calling. A healthcare demo illustrates a production use case: a voice bot calling patients to collect intake information through natural conversation with tool calling to mocked EHR systems. On speed, Kramer distinguishes throughput (generally adequate) from latency (the hard problem). Human conversational norms demand ~500ms responses; people often respond in 200-300ms. Exceeding 500ms enters the uncanny valley. The primary strategy is co-locating STT, LLM, and TTS in a single compute container rather than calling separate hosted services. Kramer provides a detailed latency breakdown: Mac OS laptop mic processing alone costs 30-40ms before any controllable software; transcription and phrase endpointing can reach a couple hundred ms; LLM time to first token ~100ms; TTS and network return add more. Optimistic total is 600-700ms. A live geography-game demo shows voice-to-voice latency of 500-700ms using Deepgram STT/TTS and Llama 3 8B, with a real-time UI displaying per-component metrics. The architecture is open-sourced. Kramer then introduces Pipecat, an open-source, vendor-neutral framework for real-time and multimodal AI orchestration, supporting conversational bots, speech-to-speech translation, voice-controlled agents, and real-time vision. Pipecat adoption surged with the GPT-4o announcement, and the demo posted on Twitter reached 175,000 views, reflecting growing interest in voice AI.

sections.title: Introduction and Early Experiments
sections.summary: Kwindla introduces himself and Daily (real-time audio/video infrastructure). Shows an early GPT-4 voice bot demo telling jokes, noting that LLMs consistently know the same jokes. The foundational goal is connecting a user's device to cloud GPUs for voice conversation.

sections.title: Architectural Complexity Map
sections.summary: Presents a detailed map of the many components required for real-time voice AI: media processing/transport, transcription, pipeline/buffer management, model swapping, external system calls, phrase endpointing, interruption handling, echo cancellation, and TTS. Emphasizes this is genuinely multimodal AI spanning low-level audio to RAG and tool calling.

sections.title: Healthcare Voice Bot Demo
sections.summary: Shows a real, unedited demo of a voice bot calling a patient to collect intake information—birthday, prescriptions with dosages, and allergies—through natural conversation. Uses real tool calling to mocked EHR systems. Illustrates how all architectural components come together to feel simple and natural.

sections.title: Latency Fundamentals and Targets
sections.summary: Distinguishes throughput (adequate for current tools) from latency (the hard problem). Human conversational norms demand ~500ms responses; people often respond in 200-300ms using native speculative prediction. Gemini Pro's time to first token is ~900ms, already nearly double the target. Model and tool selection is heavily constrained by latency requirements.

sections.title: Co-Location Strategy
sections.summary: The most powerful tool for speed is co-locating STT, phrase endpointing, LLM inference, and TTS in a single compute container. While 95-99% of GenAI uses hosted services, self-hosting with controllable tuning is necessary when latency is the priority. Begins introducing a breakdown of specific latency numbers for pipeline components.

sections.title: Detailed Latency Breakdown and Geography Game Demo
sections.summary: Provides per-component latency numbers: Mac OS laptop mic processing costs 30-40ms (echo cancellation, noise removal, gain control); audio encoding, network transport, jitter buffer, and decoding follow; transcription and phrase endpointing can reach a couple hundred ms; LLM time to first token ~100ms; TTS and return network add more. Optimistic total is 600-700ms. A live geography-game demo (fastbot) shows voice-to-voice latency of 500-700ms using Deepgram STT/TTS and Llama 3 8B, with a real-time UI displaying per-component metrics. The container is open-source. Llama 3 70B was too slow; 8B was used instead.

sections.title: Pipecat Open-Source Framework
sections.summary: Introduces Pipecat, an open-source, vendor-neutral framework for real-time and multimodal AI orchestration, analogous to LangChain/LlamaIndex for the real-time domain. Supports conversational bots, speech-to-speech translation, voice-controlled agents, and real-time vision. Pipecat adoption surged with the GPT-4o announcement; the demo posted on Twitter reached 175,000 views. Multimodal models will make building faster stuff easier but won't eliminate the need for orchestration layers.
